A constant column carries no information and is collinear with the intercept; R’s QR pivoting detects the aliasing, drops the column and prints NA for its coefficient — which is how we discovered that two of the eleven descriptors were constant. car::vif() then refuses to run until they are removed by hand.
  1. Interpret a logistic coefficient of 0.816 on a standardised descriptor.
The odds of being active multiply by exp(0.816) = 2.26 for each one-standard-deviation increase in that descriptor (here the rotatable-bond count), holding the others fixed. Report the odds ratio with its confidence interval (1.90 to 2.70), not the coefficient, and state that “holding the others fixed” is an arithmetic statement about the model, not a claim that the descriptor can be changed independently in a real molecule.
  1. Your logistic model reports a coefficient of 10.6 with a standard error of 18,560 and p = 1.000. What happened?
Separation: some predictor or combination of predictors perfectly classifies the outcome, so the likelihood has no finite maximum and glm stops at its iteration limit with the warning “fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred”. Check whether the classes are disjoint on that predictor, and use a penalised (glmnet) or Firth-corrected fit.
  1. Model A has AUC 0.705 and Brier 0.220; model B has AUC 0.705 and Brier 0.243. Which do you deploy?
A, if the predicted probabilities are used for anything — a cost calculation, a triage threshold, a screening budget. The two models rank compounds identically (that is what the equal AUC means); A’s probabilities are closer to the observed frequencies. If only the ranking is used, the choice is indifferent.
  1. Why can unpenalised OLS have a negative cross-validated R²?
Because cross-validated R² is computed on data the model has not seen, and a model with 1,325 correlated predictors fits the noise of the training set so closely (train R² 0.821) that its predictions on new compounds are worse than simply predicting the training mean (CV R² −0.506). Negative CV R² is the signature of over-fitting, and it is invisible if only the training R² is reported.
  1. The lasso selected 430 predictors. Can you write “these 430 features determine potency”?
No. Repeat the fit on bootstrap resamples: in our experiment only 130 predictors were selected in at least 80 % of resamples, while 590 appeared in a fifth or fewer and 605 sat in the unstable middle. Report selection frequencies, and remember that when predictors are correlated, the lasso picks one of them nearly arbitrarily.
  1. AIC prefers the two-descriptor model and BIC the intercept-only one. Which do you believe?
Neither automatically — they target different things (AIC approximates predictive loss, BIC approximates posterior model probability with a log n penalty) and disagreement simply means the extra parameters are worth about as much as they cost. Decide with the design and the scientific question; in a paired design, the blocking factor stays in the model whatever BIC says.
  1. What does blocking on patient do to the estimate and to its standard error in a balanced paired design?
It leaves the point estimate unchanged (−0.980 both ways) and reduces the standard error, here from 0.102 to 0.074, because between-patient variation is removed from the residual. In an unbalanced design it would also shift the estimate, which is the sense in which it “adjusts for” the patient. A mixed model with (1 | patient) achieves the same with one variance parameter instead of 68 dummies.

Glossary

Adjusted R²
R² penalised for the number of predictors; unlike R² it can decrease when a predictor is added.
AIC / BIC
Information criteria balancing fit against complexity, with penalties of 2 and log(n) per parameter; comparable only across models on identical data.
Aliased coefficient
A predictor exactly collinear with others (e.g. constant within the data); R drops it and reports NA.
Blocking
Including the identity of the experimental unit (patient, batch, plate) as a factor, removing its variation from the residual.
Calibration
Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies; measured by a reliability curve and the Brier score.
Chance correlation
Apparent fit arising from too many descriptors on too few compounds; quantified by response randomisation.
Confounder
A variable associated with both predictor and response that can create or mask an apparent effect.
Cook’s distance
Influence measure combining leverage and residual size; the change in the fit when one observation is deleted.
Elastic net
Penalty mixing L1 and L2 (glmnet with 0 < alpha < 1); keeps correlated predictors together instead of choosing one.
Hansch analysis
Classical QSAR: a linear model of potency in physicochemical substituent properties within a congeneric series.
Interaction
A product term letting the slope on one predictor depend on another; x1 * x2 in an R formula.
Intraclass correlation
Share of total variance attributable to the grouping factor of a mixed model.
Lasso
L1-penalised regression (alpha = 1); shrinks some coefficients exactly to zero, performing selection.
Leverage
How far an observation’s predictors lie from their centroid; the diagonal of the hat matrix, hatvalues().
Lambda.1se
The largest penalty whose cross-validated error is within one standard error of the minimum; cv.glmnet’s conservative default.
Logistic regression
Linear model for the log-odds of a binary outcome; coefficients exponentiate to odds ratios.
Multicollinearity
Near-linear dependence among predictors; inflates coefficient variances without harming predictions.
Normal equations
XᵀXβ = Xᵀy, whose solution is the least-squares estimate.
Odds ratio
exp(coefficient) in a logistic model; the multiplicative change in odds per unit of the predictor.
Ridge regression
L2-penalised regression (alpha = 0); shrinks all coefficients smoothly and keeps every predictor.
Separation
A predictor combination perfectly classifying the outcome, so the logistic likelihood has no finite maximum.
Stability selection
Assessing which predictors a selection method keeps across resamples of the data.
VIF
Variance inflation factor, 1/(1 − R²ⱼ); the factor by which collinearity inflates a coefficient’s variance.
y-randomisation
Permuting the response and refitting, to obtain the null distribution of a goodness-of-fit statistic.
